name: Aloesin
lead: Aloesin is a chromone glucoside isolated from the Aloe plant that has been studied as a topical skin-lightening agent because it inhibits tyrosinase, the key enzyme of melanin synthesis [4]. It is also among the best-studied active constituents of Aloe vera alongside aloe-emodin, aloin, emodin and acemannan [1].

Laboratory studies reported that aloesin competitively inhibits tyrosinase and reduces melanin production in vitro, and a 2002 study reported that it inhibited UV-induced hyperpigmentation [4][8]. Reviews of botanical skin-lightening agents discuss it alongside other plant extracts [2]. The sources reviewed contain no randomized clinical trial results for aloesin.

paras: A 2002 paper described aloesin as 2-acetonyl-8-beta-D-glucopyranosyl-7-hydroxy-5-methylchromone and reported that it modulates melanogenesis by competitive inhibition of tyrosinase, acting on purified enzyme and on melanin production in vitro; kinetic studies used mushroom, human melanocyte lysate and other tyrosinase sources [4]. A 1999 study reported that aloesin and arbutin inhibit tyrosinase in a synergistic manner through different mechanisms [10].

Aloesin derivatives, including isorabaichromone, feruloylaloesin and p-coumaroylaloesin, showed antioxidant and radical-scavenging activity in laboratory assays [3]. In animal and cell work, aloesin has been reported to accelerate wound healing through MAPK/Rho and Smad signalling [7] and dietary aloesin was examined in a rat colitis model [5]. These studies are not about appearance use in humans.

No studies found of controlled human trials of aloesin for skin lightening in the sources reviewed. The research consists of enzyme, cell and animal studies, plus a 2002 report on UV-induced hyperpigmentation [4][8].

timeline.event: Aloesin and arbutin reported to inhibit tyrosinase synergistically [10].

card.summary: An Aloe-derived tyrosinase inhibitor with lab-level evidence for lightening and no published trials found.
card.note: Evidence is enzyme, cell and UV-induced pigmentation work; no controlled trials found.

quick.overview:
Aloesin is a compound from the Aloe plant studied as a skin-lightening ingredient for dark spots.

Research is mostly in test tubes, cells and a 2002 report on UV-induced pigmentation; controlled trials in people were not found.
quick.mechanism: It competitively inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, and has been reported to act synergistically with arbutin.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed give no human safety data specific to topical aloesin; most reports concern laboratory and animal models.
